VERDICT:
Three things are settled on the part of the ladder that has run and none of
them is a threshold.

### Positional binding survives its own data fix

At 45M there are {{kpx_l45_count}} question shapes of the held-out sentence
mode where the reader is exact on {{kpx_l45_key_n}} of {{kpx_l45_key_n}}
key-first items and on 0 of {{kpx_l45_value_n}} value-first ones:
{{kpx_l45_shapes}}. Same shape, same group, same mode, same gold structures.
Only which of the two the sentence names first differs.

The seven shapes that are exact on no value-first item of that group each saw between {{keypos_seven_vf_min}} and {{keypos_seven_vf_max}}
value-first training items, {{keypos_seven_share_min}} to
{{keypos_seven_share_max}} of that shape's own draw, and between
{{keypos_seven_per_mode_min}} and {{keypos_seven_per_mode_max}} of them inside
every one of the {{n_trained_modes}} sentence modes training contained. On
those modes the reader is {{kp_l45_train_value_first}} exact on value-first
items against {{kp_l45_train_key_first}} on key-first ones, over
{{kp_l45_train_value_first_n}} and {{kp_l45_train_key_first_n}} items. It has
the order and it reads it. On a sentence mode it never saw, the same reader is
{{kp_l45_mode_value_first}} on value first against
{{kp_l45_mode_key_first}} on key first, and on seven shapes it is exact on
zero value-first items out of 93.

The binding is in the text and it is not ambiguous there. The hand-written
parser reads the same value-first half of that group
{{parser_mode_value_first}}, and {{parser_mode_lookup_value_first}} on each of
the seven shapes taken separately.

Balancing key position in the training draw cannot fix that, because the draw
is already balanced and has been all along. What failed to transfer is the
combination of an axis value the network saw about forty thousand times per
shape with an axis value it never saw at all, and no draw fixes that without
giving up the held-out test. This is a representational failure and not a
distributional one, and it is the first failure in this project that is known
to survive the data fix that would be tried on it.

### The transposed operand test is the other case and does have a data fix

Its fine tuning draw carries one operand order on
{{grid_train_canonical}} of {{grid_train_pages}} pages. Fine tuning on the
balanced draw instead takes the reading of the transposed page from
{{tp_l45_transposed_all_exact}} to {{tpb_l45_transposed_all_exact}} and the
untransposed key order from {{tp_l45_transposed_all_key_order_canonical}} to
{{tpb_l45_transposed_all_key_order_canonical}}. That one was a hole in a draw.
It costs the original version of the page,
{{tp_l45_original_all_exact}} down to {{tpb_l45_original_all_exact}}, and the
group it helps least is the held-out sentence mode, where the untransposed
order still wins {{tpb_l45_transposed_mode_key_order_canonical}} against
{{tpb_l45_transposed_mode_exact}} exact.

Under the original one-order draw the test does not move with scale at all. On
the `train` frame group the fine tuned reader is exact on the original page
{{tp_l45_original_train_exact}} at 45M and {{tp_xl93_original_train_exact}} at
93M, so it has the page shape, and on the transposed version of that same page
it is exact {{tp_l45_transposed_train_exact}} and
{{tp_xl93_transposed_train_exact}} while writing the untransposed key order
{{tp_l45_transposed_train_key_order_canonical}} and
{{tp_xl93_transposed_train_key_order_canonical}}. Doubling the parameters moved
none of it.

### What would decide whether it is general

The reading above is that the reader has the value-first order on every
sentence mode it trained on and loses it on one it did not. It does not say
whether that is about `relative_clause` in particular or about any unseen mode.
`src/norm/ndata.py` withholds the mode through one constant, `HELD_MODE`, so
the check is that constant, a rebuild of `data/norm`, one rung at 30,000 steps
and the same scoring, which is about three hours on this card. If a different
withheld mode also produces shapes exact on every key-first item and no
value-first one, the failure is a property of the architecture and not of one
sentence form.

### What the ladder can and cannot say about parameters

The rungs share a token budget, not a budget per parameter. {{budget_steps}}
steps at a {{budget_cap}} source-token cap is {{budget_source_tokens}} source
tokens and {{budget_target_tokens}} target tokens for every rung, which is
{{tpp_l45_source}} source tokens per parameter at 45M against
{{tpp_xl93_source}} at 93M. Counting only the tokens the loss falls on it is
{{tpp_l45_target}} against {{tpp_xl93_target}}. Whichever count is used, the
93M rung had half the tokens per parameter the 45M rung had.

At that budget, and at the 45M rung's own rate, the 93M rung fits its own
training file worse than the 45M rung, {{tail_xl93lr40_5000}} against
{{tail_l45_5000}} over the last 5,000 steps, and reads worse on four of the
five frame groups. A larger model fitting its own training data worse at
matched steps is the signature of undertraining. What that pair measures is
that at a fixed token budget doubling the parameters costs, which is what a
scaling law predicts, and it is a different statement from the one this ladder
was built to make.

So the claim that more parameters do not buy surface generalisation here is
not supported by the pair and is not made. `xl93match` is the run that
separates the two readings: the same rung at the same rate for
{{steps_match_xl93}} steps, which is the 45M rung's tokens per parameter
rather than its step count, and nothing else changed. If it then beats the 45M
rung on the trained and held-out-question groups, the parameter axis was
always fine and the earlier reading was undertraining. If it beats the 45M
rung everywhere except the held-out sentence mode, that is the dissociation
worth having, and it is much stronger than what is here now, because the
larger model would then be better at everything except the compositional axis.

One caveat on the arithmetic itself. The run makes {{budget_epochs}} passes
over a file of {{budget_examples}} examples, so these are not unique tokens
and the usual tokens-per-parameter guidance, which assumes they are, applies
loosely. The undertraining reading does not rest on that guidance. It rests on
the direct observation that at equal steps the larger rung fit its own
training data less well, and more steps at the same rate is the direct remedy
for that.

### Two of the four rungs cannot reach a comparable budget on this card

{{TOKEN_BUDGET}}

At the 45M rung's tokens per parameter the 167M rung needs
{{steps_match_xxl167}} steps and the 355M rung {{steps_match_xxxl355}}. On one
L40S that is about fourteen hours and about sixty-four. The 167M rung is
queued at its matched budget and runs last. The 355M rung is not run at all.
A 355M rung reported as flat after seeing an eighth of the tokens per
parameter the 45M rung saw would be a statement about its budget that reads as
a statement about the architecture, and that is worse than leaving the top of
the ladder empty.

The ladder therefore does not reach 350M, and the question of where surface
generalisation appears between 45M and 350M is not answered here. What is
answered is narrower and is the part the card can pay for.
